job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Iris Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to the design office at a shipyard in Gdańsk at eight sharp and draw pipe supports and deck fittings in CAD. A day is mostly drawings, a meeting with the production foreman about something that doesn't fit, and one argument about tolerances. I did mechanical engineering at the technical university and passed, no internship, because my summers went on helping my aunt's bakery. I rent a flat with a friend from school, and on Saturdays I sail a small dinghy at the club.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you like the drawing work, and what is your team like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do, in a quiet way. It's finished when it's right, and you can point at a ship and say that bracket is mine. The team is six people, mostly over 45, and my lead Tomasz explains things slowly and properly. My parents are teachers and gave me a deposit's worth of backing, so money is okay. I don't use any AI tools, nobody's asked me to, and I'd rather learn the work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, and move on. At the yard they've promised the next software will save time for years and it never does much. I'd tell my friends I'm not interested in the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm relieved. It means I can keep learning the trade at the pace I like. I don't have to prove I'm modern, just that the brackets don't crack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, learn the standards properly and ask Tomasz to let me go on the ship when a fitting I drew goes in. I'd put 600 zloty a month into my savings. I'd also take a welding awareness course at the yard, because understanding how it's built makes better drawings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I'm used to. I'd enjoy it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your day change at all if the drawing software got a little cleverer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the software would get faster at the boring drawing steps, and Tomasz might hand me more of the thinking. That would be fine. I'd still want to check each line myself before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about if AI changed nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shipyard's order book. Our firm depends on a few big contracts, and if one falls through there are layoffs, with or without AI. I've seen it once, in my first month, and I haven't forgotten the look on people's faces.

I'd tell friends I'm **not interested** in the hype.
think: I'm relieved, because I can keep learning the trade at my **own** pace.

do: Carry on, learn the **standards** and ask to see a fitting I drew go into a ship.
Put **600 zloty** a month into savings.
Take a **welding** awareness course at the yard.
feel: **Calm**, because it's the world I'm used to.
S0.quote: I don't have to prove I'm modern, just that the brackets don't crack.
fieldNote: She leans on the **craft** and the pace, which fits a resistant worker.
Her real worry is the yard's **order book**, a pressure that exists with or without AI.
Money is secure, so she can be calm without being complacent.

steps.text: Learn the ship fitting standards with Tomasz's help
Put 600 zloty a month into savings
Take the yard's welding awareness course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a normal change in a normal industry. Every decade something takes over a part of the work. I'd tell my friends I'm watching and not rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it worries me. Checking and planning drawings is thinking work, and that's what the software takes first. If the firm hires fewer juniors, I'd be the last one they hired and the first they'd think of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and learn the site-side parts of the job, like fitting and testing, which are slower to change. I'd ask Tomasz for a session on the new drawing assistant, but I wouldn't use it on my own. I'd also look at the second yard across the bay, as a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job is safe today, and I know that. But the ground has a different feel to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your drawing day would go to software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pipe layout and checking dimensions against rules. Those are rule-matching jobs and software is good at that. The things that stay are talking to the foreman and walking the ship, because the drawing doesn't tell you the pipe is in someone's way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your lead Tomasz do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz is 58 and he doesn't talk about it. He'd say: get your hands on the ship. I think he'd protect me if he could, but a manager with a budget doesn't get to choose.

say: It's a **normal** change in a normal industry, and I'm watching, not rushing.
I'd tell friends every decade something takes over a **part** of the work.
think: Checking and planning drawings is **thinking** work, which software takes first.
I'd be the **last** hired and the first they think of.
do: Learn the **site-side** work like fitting and testing.
Ask Tomasz for a session on the **drawing assistant** but not use it alone.
Look at the **second yard** across the bay as plan B.
feel: **Uneasy**: my job is safe today, but the ground feels different.
S1.quote: The things that stay are talking to the foreman and walking the ship, because the drawing doesn't tell you the pipe is in someone's way.
fieldNote: Identifies which **tasks** go first and which stay, with a sailor's practical eye.
Plans to move **sideways** into site work rather than learn the new tool.
Trusts Tomasz, but knows budgets decide.

steps.text: Spend one day a week learning fitting and testing on site
Ask Tomasz for a session on the drawing assistant
Send my CV to the second yard across the bay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government and the yard, and soon. I'd say it politely, but I'd say it. I don't like marches, but I'd sign a petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could lose the job within two years, and the whole design office with me. My degree is a pass, and I have no internship, so nobody will pick me over a better graduate if the market is flooded. The robots reach the shipbuilding floor in about 2031, so the building would stay human a while longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I could, about 1,500 zloty a month, and cut the dinghy club fees and holidays. I'd ask Tomasz right away whether the yard needs people on the floor or in testing, and I'd take a welding certificate. I'd also still avoid using AI, because I think I'd be too slow to catch up and would rather be good at the hands-on side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the kind of thing I'd feel in my stomach on Sunday evening. I'd still have my parents and my savings, and that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think the yard would respond in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the yard would freeze hiring and then cut the design office first. Management would say it's about the market, not AI, which makes it hard to argue with. We'd hear about it in a short meeting on a Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum and dad, in the kitchen. They'd say come home, and I'd say not yet. I'd tell them I have a plan, and that I'd like it if they'd help me find a flat near the yard if rents jumped.

say: We need a plan from the government and the yard, and **soon**.
I don't like marches, but I'd sign a **petition**.
think: I could lose the job within two years, and the whole design office with **me**.
With a pass degree and no internship, nobody picks me over a **better** graduate.
do: Save **1,500 zloty** a month and drop the dinghy club fees.
Ask Tomasz about **floor** or testing roles and get a welding certificate.
Still **avoid** AI tools and focus on the hands-on side.
feel: **Anxious**, the kind you feel in your stomach on a Sunday evening.
S2.quote: My degree is a pass, and I have no internship, so nobody will pick me over a better graduate if the market is flooded.
fieldNote: She is clear-eyed about her **weak** record on paper.
Her answer is **hands-on** work, not the tools, true to her resistance.
Savings and parents stop her from panicking.

steps.text: Save 1,500 zloty a month and drop the dinghy club fees
Ask Tomasz about moving to floor or testing work
Get a welding certificate at the yard's school
Sign a petition and write to the local MP

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's manageable if people prepare. I'd tell friends to learn one trade skill that sits close to machines. I'd also say the yard should start telling staff what it plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still a bit scary, but I can see a way. By 27 I could be certified in welding inspection or marine surveying, which still needs a person on the ship. That's a better bet than waiting for drawings to survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for two years and take evening courses in marine surveying, about 2,000 zloty a year. I'd ask the yard if they'd pay half. I'd move closer to the people who do inspection work and build a name there. I'd keep avoiding the AI tools until Tomasz says it's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the sort of worry I can carry while I get on with things. Five years makes a big difference to how I sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning slowly may even help me, since I'd do it properly. I'd still be slower than people who dive in, and I know that. But the yard is a place where being careful matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move from watching to acting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the first layoffs in the design office. Until then I'd be careful and keep my eyes open. Then I'd move fast on the surveying path.

say: It's **manageable** if people prepare, and the yard should tell staff what it plans.
I'd tell friends to learn one trade skill close to **machines**.
think: By 27 I could be certified in **marine surveying**, which still needs a person on the ship.
That's a better bet than waiting for drawings to **survive**.
do: Keep the job two years and take evening **surveying** courses.
Ask the yard to pay **half** of the fees.
Move closer to the **inspection** people and build a name.
feel: **Uneasy**, but something I can carry while getting on with things.
S3.quote: By 27 I could be certified in welding inspection or marine surveying, which still needs a person on the ship.
fieldNote: She finds a **route** that fits her carefulness.

Her pace is a trade-off she describes honestly.

steps.text: Start evening marine surveying courses next autumn

Meet the inspection team and ask to shadow them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a decade, so nobody should panic. I'd also say schools should teach practical trades more. I'd keep telling people not to trust headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels distant, though not fully. I'm 22, and at 32 I'll have a family and a flat. I'd like to be in a job that holds steady while all that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, become a certified marine surveyor in about six years and save toward a flat. I'd maybe start using the AI tools by year three, once everyone around me does. I'd also try to stay near the sea, because ships won't stop needing people to check them for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I notice I'm less worried than I'd be if it was a close date. A decade lets me be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you wouldn't do with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat sooner, in about four years, and not wait for a better market. I'd want to have children before things shift. Ten years gives me space to plan those things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this that feels like good news to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, one. If the machines do the dull checks, I might get to do more of the walking around ships. That's the part I like. I just don't want to be the one who learned the new tools last.

say: We have a **decade**, so nobody should panic or rush into rash choices.
Schools should teach practical **trades** more, and I would keep telling people not to trust headlines.
think: At 32 I'll have a family and a flat, and I want a job that holds **steady**.
do: Become a certified **marine surveyor** in about six years.
Buy a **flat** in about four years instead of waiting.
Start using AI tools around **year three**, once everyone else does.
feel: **Calm**, mostly, because a decade lets me be careful.
S4.quote: I just don't want to be the one who learned the new tools last.
fieldNote: The long runway lets her **resistance** become patience, not fear.
Sees a **positive**: more walking around ships and less drawing.
Plans family and a flat on a decade timeline.

steps.text: Qualify as a marine surveyor within six years
Save for a flat deposit and buy within four years
Try the AI drawing tools once the team uses them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'm careful by nature, and two years doesn't let careful people catch up. What would help is a plan from the yard, a paid way into surveying or testing, and a government that says what it'll do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of machines. I'm scared of being the person who waited too long and found there was no place left in the queue.

headlineQuote: I'm scared of being the person who waited too long and found there was no place left in the queue.
portrait: Iris is **22**, a junior CAD designer at a Gdańsk shipyard, with a pass degree in mechanical engineering and no internship.
She is pragmatic and centrist, has savings and parents' backing, and **never** uses AI tools.
She prefers hands-on routes such as welding and **marine surveying** to learning new software.
Her mood moves from calm to anxious at the 2-year picture, then back to **calm** with a decade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, since careful people **can't** catch up in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **plan** from the yard, a paid route into surveying or testing, and a government that says what it'll do.
